claims.text: In high-entropy superconducting alloys, Tc is governed primarily by the density of states at the Fermi level rather than by chemical disorder.
(TaNb)₁₋ₓ(ZrHfTi)ₓ films exhibit substantial atomic-scale disorder.
(TaNb)₁₋ₓ(ZrHfTi)ₓ superconducting films are in the dirty limit.
Controlled annealing can reduce chemical disorder or improve short-range order without changing composition or inducing secondary phases.
Annealing can reduce quenched disorder while avoiding grain growth, phase separation, and significant compositional redistribution.
Changes in local atomic order and short-range chemical environments tune the electronic band structure and the DOS at the Fermi level.
The superconducting behavior of the specified HEA films is consistent with a conventional BCS description.
Within a classical BCS framework, changes in the DOS at the Fermi level can produce changes in Tc.
Disorder-induced electron scattering in the as-grown films is already saturated.
Because disorder-induced scattering is saturated, reducing disorder by annealing should not significantly change Tc.
Annealing-induced changes in local order may modestly alter pairing through changes in the DOS.
Annealing-induced local ordering may narrow the superconducting transition.
Annealed films should exhibit only minimal shifts in Tc relative to as-grown films.
Annealed films should exhibit only minimal changes in coherence length relative to as-grown films.
Annealing may sharpen the superconducting transition.
Annealing should not produce a significant change in the electron scattering rate.
If disorder governed superconductivity, reducing disorder by annealing would cause large changes in Tc and scattering parameters.
Films with substantially different compositions and Tc can have comparable mean free paths of about 5–6 nm, so their observed Tc variation is not supported as disorder-driven.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conventional dirty-limit BCS HEAs for which annealing does not appreciably change composition, grain size, or phase constitution.
A large annealing-induced change in Tc or scattering rate attributable to reduced disorder would falsify DOS dominance.
